items.title: Can’t Patch PHP2Shell Yet? Build a Stopgap with the Controls You Own
items.summary: PHP2Shell comes with a clear instruction: update PHP. Fixed releases exist for supported branches, and Qualys customers can identify PHP installations using network scans, Cloud Agents, container assessments, and Deep Scan where supported, while assessing exposed web applications and APIs with Qualys TotalAppSec. Patching at this scale still takes time. In Qualys telemetry, only 199,000 of the 156 million PHP package installations with a known version had been patched during the first 12 hours after disclosure. Those first days are where mitigations and compensating controls earn their place. They reduce risk while updates roll out, and the right visibility shows which servers need attention first. Our PHP2Shell guide covers detection and fixed versions. Here is how to bridge the gap between disclosure and patch. Start with Qualys Mitigation Qualys provides a configuration-level mitigation for PHP2Shell based on PHP’s guidance and insights from the Qualys Threat Research Unit. It disables session upload progress and hardens related session-handling configuration on supported hosts. This reduces exposure to the confirmed session-lifecycle attack path without requiring application-code changes. It does not eliminate every exploitation path associated with the two CVEs. Applications that depend on upload-progress functionality should be tested after the change. Configuration-level, with restart verification . The mitigation applies configuration changes and automatically restarts the PHP service. Review the execution logs and restart the service manually if a restart is still required. Confirm that every affected PHP worker has picked up the new configuration. Verified, not assumed. After the restart, Qualys checks the effective configuration to confirm the setting is active and not overridden elsewhere. With or without an agent. Customers with vulnerable detections can select Mitigate Now from their dashboards. For appliances, DMZ servers, and legacy hosts that cannot run a Cloud Agent, the same mitigation script is available in the Custom Assessment and Remediation (CAR) library in TruRisk Eliminate and runs directly on scanner-based hosts. Ready when the patch is. You can deploy supported vendor patches through TruRisk Eliminate. Qualys reports a High patch reliability rating for these updates and no OS reboot requirement for this PHP package update. Restart every service that loads PHP and verify that its workers are running the patched build. Mitigation reduces risk in the interim. Updating remains the only complete fix. Add Layers from the Security Stack You Already Run The tools already in your environment can work alongside the mitigation, each at a different point in the attack path. Network and application protection: WAF and IPS. Vendors including Akamai, Cloudflare, F5, Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet, and Check Point have published PHP2Shell protections. Coverage varies by product, CVE, signature, and configuration. These protections can block known exploit requests; some, including Cloudflare’s, also inspect and block malicious responses. Keep signatures current and confirm that the relevant traffic is inspected and blocking is enabled. Cloudflare has reported attempts to bypass its protections, so treat these controls as additional layers while patching proceeds. After exploitation: EDR. Endpoint controls can provide visibility into suspicious child processes, malicious command execution, and web-shell deployment. CrowdStrike Falcon and Cortex XDR document PHP2Shell-related post-exploitation protections. For Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and other tools, verify the applicable platform support and enabled policies before claiming specific coverage. These layers can detect or block different stages of an attack, but they do not guarantee that every exploitation attempt will be stopped. Each layer catches what the one before it might miss. PHP2Shell 3rd-party mitigation and compensating controls PHP2Shell 3rd-party mitigation and compensating controls Select the WAF, IPS, and EDR you run to see the exact signatures and policies each vendor has released for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, ready to copy into your console. Edge WAF None Akamai Cloudflare F5 BIG-IP FortiWeb WAF None Network IPS None Palo Alto Networks FortiGate Check Point Trend Vision One IPS None Host EDR None CrowdStrike Defender Cortex XDR SentinelOne Cybereason EDR None Platform Linux Windows macOS This interactive view needs JavaScript. Signatures covering both CVEs: Akamai 3000991; Cloudflare seven managed rules; F5 BIG-IP 200204113, 200103697, 200204115; FortiWeb 1002017614, 1002017615; Palo Alto Networks 543004, 97622 to 97625; FortiGate 62657, 62658; Check Point CPAI-2026-15172, 15184, 15224; Trend Vision One 1012749, 1012754. Endpoint policies are listed for CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Cortex XDR, SentinelOne and Cybereason. Note: Rule and policy IDs are as published by each vendor in October 2026; confirm them in your console. The endpoint policies act after exploitation and are mapped to the attacker’s next step, not to the CVEs themselves, so verify each one fires for your PHP worker. Compensating controls reduce risk; updating PHP remains the only complete fix. Give Your Controls Credit in Qualys ETM Two servers can run the same unpatched PHP build and carry very different risk. One sits behind a WAF rule that names both CVEs, with EDR watching its web server process. The other faces the internet with nothing in front of it. A version-based check can report the same vulnerability on both assets, even though their exposure and compensating controls differ. Qualys ETM is being extended to close that gap. It arrives in three steps: Recommendations on every finding. ETM will show which applicable third-party controls can reduce exposure for each vulnerability, so teams know what to enable and where. Controls reflected in the score. Controls that are in place will lower a finding’s QVSS score to reflect your actual defenses, shown as the Environmental score, so remediation queues focus on what still needs attention. Action from the same platform. Teams will be able to apply third-party mitigations through TruRisk Eliminate, from the platform that found the exposure. Validate the Tested Entry Point with TruConfirm TruConfirm helps validate indicators of the tested PHP2Shell entry point. According to Qualys’s PHP2Shell guide , its benign probe checks for behavior indicating that the entry point is reachable and the upload-progress mitigation is absent, without creating files, executing code, or applying memory pressure. Qualys reports that, in one customer environment with 1,539 assets running PHP, TruConfirm returned positive validation results for 25 assets. These findings help prioritize investigation and remediation. A negative result does not establish that every exploitation path is closed. After mitigation or patching, repeat the validation and separately verify the effective configuration, installed packages, and running PHP workers. Where to Start Use QID 45110 to support PHP discovery, then use the applicable vulnerability detection QIDs and software inventory to assess assets in scope. Use TruConfirm results alongside internet exposure and business criticality to prioritize remediation. Apply the supported Qualys mitigation workflow to systems awaiting an update, using agent-based or scanner-based execution as applicable. Verify the effective configuration and required restarts.Keep applicable WAF, IPS, and EDR protections enabled and current as additional layers. Deploy the appropriate PHP or vendor update, restart every service that loads PHP, verify the running patched build, and repeat the relevant validation checks. Compensating controls buy valuable time, but they do not remove the flaw. Keep tracking every system until it is patched. Not a Qualys customer yet? Sign up for the free PHP2Shell mitigation service .

items.title: Hacker Exploits Critical PHP2Shell Flaws to Win $2,000 Bitcoin Challenge, Releases PoC
items.summary: A security researcher known online as killa has won a public Bitcoin challenge by using two critical PHP flaws to reach a test server. The winning run took 19.28 hours. The prize pot was 0.02511679 BTC, worth $2,021.22 at the time of the win on October 25, 2026, at 15:47 UTC. The researcher then published a proof of concept (PoC) on GitHub. The challenge ran on stealmybitcoin.com. The site used unpatched PHP and held a wallet key behind a remote code execution test, which means the goal was to run commands on the server from the outside. Donations pushed the prize from $500 to more than $2,000 while the test ran. The creator said early tries failed because the server first served static files through PHP’s command-line mode, which skipped the bugs. After the site moved to a real PHP page, the test became possible. PHP2Shell Flaws Exploited The bugs are tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 , and the group is called PHP2Shell. Both carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, which is rated critical. The first bug can corrupt memory during cleanup after an out-of-memory condition. The second lets data left by an earlier request in a shared worker be reused by a later request. PHP released fixes on October 21, 2026, in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Google’s guidance says the affected range covers PHP 5.4 through 8.5.11. Older branches such as 8.1 and earlier no longer get official fixes, so those sites need to move to a supported version. The public script uses two memory leaks. The first leak reveals a heap address, and the second reveals a PHP code address. With both addresses, a final request places a forged structure in memory that leads PHP to call its system function. The script then prints a random test marker, the user ID, and the hash of the flag program. The write-up also shows the limits of the work. The script was built and tested against a local lab copy, not the live site, and it succeeded in about seven of ten lab runs. The author admits that the full live request was not captured. The recovered key also did not match the advertised prize address, and the author called that a mistake on the creator’s side. Public exploit code is now available , and hacking activity started before the patches. Amazon reported attempts dating back to October 17, four days before the fixes. Sophos said it blocked attempts to deliver Potassium, a likely Mirai botnet variant, but it found no proof of a successful compromise. Upgrading to a patched PHP release is the only full fix. Firewall rules and configuration changes may reduce risk, but they do not close the flaws. After upgrading, restart services and confirm that the active workers run the new build, because bundled runtimes and containers may still use old code. For more background, read our earlier coverage of the PHP2Shell vulnerability and public PoC and the PHP emergency patch release . Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.summary_html:
A security researcher known online as killa has won a public Bitcoin challenge by using two critical PHP flaws to reach a test server. The winning run took 19.28 hours. The prize pot was 0.02511679 BTC, worth $2,021.22 at the time of the win on October 25, 2026, at 15:47 UTC. The researcher then published a proof of concept (PoC) on GitHub.

The challenge ran on stealmybitcoin.com. The site used unpatched PHP and held a wallet key behind a remote code execution test, which means the goal was to run commands on the server from the outside.

Donations pushed the prize from $500 to more than $2,000 while the test ran. The creator said early tries failed because the server first served static files through PHP’s command-line mode, which skipped the bugs. After the site moved to a real PHP page, the test became possible.

PHP2Shell Flaws Exploited

The bugs are tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and the group is called PHP2Shell. Both carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, which is rated critical. The first bug can corrupt memory during cleanup after an out-of-memory condition. The second lets data left by an earlier request in a shared worker be reused by a later request.

PHP released fixes on October 21, 2026, in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Google’s guidance says the affected range covers PHP 5.4 through 8.5.11. Older branches such as 8.1 and earlier no longer get official fixes, so those sites need to move to a supported version.

The public script uses two memory leaks. The first leak reveals a heap address, and the second reveals a PHP code address. With both addresses, a final request places a forged structure in memory that leads PHP to call its system function. The script then prints a random test marker, the user ID, and the hash of the flag program.

The write-up also shows the limits of the work. The script was built and tested against a local lab copy, not the live site, and it succeeded in about seven of ten lab runs. The author admits that the full live request was not captured. The recovered key also did not match the advertised prize address, and the author called that a mistake on the creator’s side.

Public exploit code is now available, and hacking activity started before the patches. Amazon reported attempts dating back to October 17, four days before the fixes. Sophos said it blocked attempts to deliver Potassium, a likely Mirai botnet variant, but it found no proof of a successful compromise.

Upgrading to a patched PHP release is the only full fix. Firewall rules and configuration changes may reduce risk, but they do not close the flaws. After upgrading, restart services and confirm that the active workers run the new build, because bundled runtimes and containers may still use old code.

For more background, read our earlier coverage of the PHP2Shell vulnerability and public PoC and the PHP emergency patch release.
